report.tagline: Google's free mobile operating system that runs on most of the world's phones, made by Samsung, Xiaomi, Vivo and hundreds of other brands.
report.simpleSummary: Android is the software that makes most smartphones work: the home screen, settings, notifications and app store. Google gives it free to phone makers like Samsung, Xiaomi, Vivo and Nothing, which is why phones from ₹6,000 to ₹1.5 lakh all run it. Google makes money because those phones come with Google Search, YouTube, Gemini and the Play Store, where Google takes a cut of app sales. In India, about 9 in 10 smartphones run Android.

overview.whatItDoes: Android is an open-source operating system for phones, tablets, TVs, watches and cars. Google develops it and releases a new version each year. Phone makers can use the free open-source code, but most also license Google Mobile Services (Play Store, Search, Maps, YouTube, Gemini), which comes with rules on what they must pre-install.
howItWorks: Google builds Android and releases the code as the Android Open Source Project.
Phone makers add their own skins, like Samsung One UI or Xiaomi HyperOS, and sell phones at every price.
To ship the Play Store, makers sign agreements with Google and pre-install Google apps.
Users download apps from Google Play; Google takes a service fee on paid apps and in-app purchases.
Google shares some search ad revenue with phone makers and carriers for setting Google as default.
Security updates come from Google, but each maker decides how long it supports each phone.
overview.valueProposition: For phone makers: a free, ready-made operating system with a huge app store. For users: choice of phones at any price. For Google: billions of people using its search, ads and services.

businessModel.summary: Google gives Android away for free and makes money from what runs on it: Search ads, YouTube ads, Play Store fees, Gemini subscriptions and Pixel phones. Android exists mainly to make sure Google's services are on billions of phones and that Apple cannot control mobile access to search.

revenueStreams.detail: Google Search, Chrome and Discover on Android generate ad revenue; the biggest benefit.
Service fees of 10% to 20% on digital purchases plus a 5% billing fee in some regions.
Google's own phones, watches and earbuds.
Google One and Google AI Pro, often sold to Android users.

businessModel.pricing: Free for phone makers (open source); Google Mobile Services licence has terms and requirements. Play Store: 20% service fee on new in-app purchase installs, 10% on subscriptions, separate 5% billing fee in US, UK and EEA from 2026.
costDrivers: Revenue share payments to phone makers and carriers
businessModel.unitEconomics: Take one Android user in India. Google earns from them through search ads, YouTube ads and the occasional Play purchase, perhaps a few hundred rupees a year, much less than a US user. The extra cost to support that user on Android is close to zero, because the software is already built and phone makers pay for the hardware. In the US, Play fees on a ₹1,000 monthly subscription would be about ₹100 service fee. Android works because billions of low-revenue users, at near-zero cost each, add up to huge ad income.

growth.moat: Android's moat is its ecosystem: billions of users attract developers, and millions of apps attract users and phone makers. A new OS would need both at once, as Microsoft found with Windows Phone. Only Apple, and Huawei's HarmonyOS in China, compete at scale.

competitors.name: Apple iOS
competitors.positioning: Premium, tightly controlled OS on iPhones.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Android runs on many brands at every price; iOS has fewer, pricier phones with longer updates and higher spending users.

competitors.positioning: Huawei's own OS, growing in China.

pmLessons: Giving a product away can be a strategy when it protects a bigger business, like Google Search.
Platforms win when both sides grow together: users bring developers, developers bring users.
Openness has trade-offs: more choice but less control over quality and updates.
Regulation can reshape a business model; Play fees changed because of courts, not customers.

interviewQuestions.question: Why does Google give Android away for free?
interviewQuestions.hint: Distribution for Search and services, defence against Apple, ecosystem. Explain the money flow.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you reduce Android fragmentation?
interviewQuestions.hint: Define it, causes (makers, cost), levers (Project Mainline style updates, rules, incentives). Metric: devices on recent patches.

interviewQuestions.question: Design Android for first-time users in rural India.
interviewQuestions.hint: Persona, top tasks (WhatsApp, UPI, YouTube), voice-first, local language, low storage. Measure setup completion.

interviewQuestions.question: Play fees were cut by regulators. How should Google respond?
interviewQuestions.hint: Value Play gives (trust, discovery, billing). Compete on service, not lock-in. Track Play billing share.

interviewQuestions.question: What is Android's north star metric?
interviewQuestions.hint: Active devices on secure software. Break into devices, update coverage, app ecosystem, engagement.
